question: Do oats count as gluten?
decision: Yes, unless labeled gluten-free
rationale: Oats are usually grown and milled next to wheat, so most contain gluten; only oats labeled gluten-free are tested.

question: Does gelatin (Jell-O, marshmallows) rule out vegetarian?
decision: Yes: gelatin counts as meat
rationale: Gelatin is made from animal skin and bones, usually pork or beef. Agar is the plant alternative and is excepted.
source: The Vegetarian Society (gelatin is made from animal skin, bones and connective tissue)

question: Does a plain "nut" set the peanut flag?
decision: Yes, as a caution
rationale: Unspecified nuts may be peanuts (often sold in mixed nuts). Named tree nuts (pine nut, cashew nut ...) are excepted.
source: FDA: peanuts are legumes and a separate major allergen from tree nuts (FALCPA)

question: Does an alternative ("maple syrup or honey") set the flag?
decision: Yes
rationale: A cook may pick either ingredient, so the recipe can contain it. A filter that guessed the safe option could serve the unsafe one.
source: Safe-direction rule of the safety filter (6.3)

question: Does unspecified "seafood" set fish and shellfish?
decision: Yes: fish, crustaceans and molluscs (see P10)
rationale: A seafood mix can contain fish, crustaceans and molluscs. "Seafood seasoning" and "seafood sauce" are excepted.
source: EU Regulation 1169/2011 Annex II lists fish, crustaceans and molluscs separately

question: Should "rawa" or "sooji" (semolina) set gluten?
decision: Yes
rationale: Rawa and sooji are Indian names for wheat semolina.

question: Hugging Face recipes: does a missing "X-free" label set the flag?
decision: Yes (safe direction)
flags_affected: contains_gluten; contains_dairy; contains_egg; contains_peanut; contains_tree_nut; contains_fish; contains_shellfish; contains_crustacean; contains_mollusc; contains_soy
rationale: The dataset computes these labels from the full ingredient lines; when it does not call a recipe X-free, we flag it rather than risk a miss. It has no separate crustacean or mollusc label, so a missing "shellfish-free" sets both.

question: What counts as red meat and what as white meat?
decision: Red meat = meat from mammals, pork and offal included (rabbit too). White meat = poultry. Fish and shellfish are their own groups, not white meat.
rationale: USDA counts all livestock (beef, veal, pork, lamb) as red meat, and treats seafood as separate from meat. WHO / IARC defines red meat as mammalian muscle meat, including organ meat.

question: What counts as processed meat?
decision: Meat that is cured, salted, smoked or fermented (bacon, ham, sausages, salami, jerky, hot dogs), poultry products included
rationale: WHO / IARC definition; processed meat is the category linked to colorectal cancer.

question: Should shellfish be split into crustaceans and molluscs?
decision: Yes: contains_crustacean and contains_mollusc, and contains_shellfish stays as either one. Unspecified seafood sets both; oyster sauce counts as mollusc
rationale: The EU, UK, Canada, Australia / NZ, Japan and Korea label them separately, and many people allergic to one can eat the other. The US list means crustaceans only.
source: EU Regulation 1169/2011 Annex II; FDA FALCPA; Health Canada priority allergens; FSANZ

question: What is not kosher (or Adventist 'clean') besides pork and shellfish?
decision: Fish without fins and scales (catfish, eel, shark, monkfish, swordfish, sturgeon and its caviar); rabbit, horse, camel and other unclean land animals; insect-based carmine
rationale: Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14. Swordfish and sturgeon lose their scales as adults, so major kosher agencies treat them as not kosher.
source: Leviticus 11; Adventist Biblical Research Institute, Clean and unclean meats

question: Do mustard greens and celery-based mixes count?
decision: Yes: mustard greens, mirepoix and Old Bay seasoning count
rationale: UK guidance treats mustard leaves as a possible allergen source; mirepoix and Old Bay are mostly celery or celery salt.
source: UK Food Standards Agency allergen guidance

question: What does contains_sulfites mean?
decision: May contain sulfites: wine, sherry, dried apricots, golden raisins, maraschino cherries and other usually sulfited ingredients
rationale: Labels only require sulfites above 10 mg/kg, which a recipe cannot measure, so the flag marks ingredients that usually carry added sulfites. Unsulfured products are excepted.

question: Does falafel count as fava beans?
decision: Yes, unless the recipe lists chickpeas instead (safe direction for G6PD deficiency)
rationale: Egyptian falafel (ta'ameya) is made from fava beans; Levantine falafel from chickpeas. Greek 'fava' (split peas) is also counted, on the safe side.

question: What counts as coffee or tea?
decision: Coffee, espresso and tea (black, green, matcha, chai), decaf included; herbal teas and dishes only named after them (coffee cake, tea cake) do not
rationale: The Latter-day Saint guidance is about coffee and tea themselves, not caffeine, so decaf counts and herbal infusions do not.

question: Is asafoetida (hing) part of the onion and garlic flag?
decision: No: it has its own flag, used by the Mahayana Buddhist profile
rationale: Mahayana Buddhists avoid it as one of the five pungent plants, but Jain and many Hindu cooks use it instead of onion and garlic.

question: What do the medical profiles promise?
decision: Only that none of the listed ingredients appear. They are screens to discuss with a doctor or dietitian, never medical advice
flags_affected: alpha_gal_friendly; pregnancy_friendly; g6pd_friendly; gout_friendly; low_tyramine; nightshade_free
rationale: Amounts, preparation and personal tolerance matter. Soft cheese counts even when baked, and smoked salmon, homemade eggnog and tiramisu count as raw, until cooking information from notebook 02 is used.
source: CDC (alpha-gal); FDA / EPA fish advice; FDA food safety for pregnant women

question: Do flavor extracts (vanilla extract about 35% alcohol) and other halal open questions count?
decision: Not decided: extracts have their own flag (contains_alcohol_extract) and halal_friendly ignores it for now. Also open: insect carmine, animal rennet in cheese, and shrimp and molluscs for the Hanafi school
rationale: Scholars differ: many accept extracts because the alcohol is a solvent and mostly evaporates, others do not. Cooking does not remove all alcohol (USDA: 85% stays when added to boiling liquid, 40% after 15 minutes of simmering, 5% after 2.5 hours).
source: USDA Table of Nutrient Retention Factors, Release 6 (2007)

question: Do truffles count as mushrooms?
decision: Savory truffles (truffle oil, black or white truffle) do; chocolate truffles do not
rationale: Truffles are fungi; a chocolate truffle is a sweet named for its shape.

question: Does a ready-made ingredient count when only the dish name mentions it?
decision: No: COMPOUND_INGREDIENTS count only in the ingredient list
rationale: A name such as "Vegan Cookies" or "Pesto Pasta" describes the dish, not a store-bought product; counting it would mark homemade vegan cookies as dairy. Plain keywords ("Mussels in Wine") still count in names.

question: When does Open Food Facts evidence suggest a hidden allergen?
decision: When at least 60% of at least 5 products whose name matches the ingredient declare it; a person may also approve an entry below that line, with the reason in the notes
rationale: Product data is entered by volunteers and name matches can pick up other foods, so one product is not enough. Below the line, a well-known risk can still be approved (asafoetida: compounded hing is cut with wheat flour).
source: Open Food Facts allergens_tags (volunteer data, ODbL)

question: Who may approve a policy or an evidence decision?
decision: A named team member. A review done by an AI assistant is recorded with its name in reviewed_by or decided_by and does not count as the human sign-off
rationale: An AI checking an AI is not independent; the record must show who decided.

question: Do wines named without the word "wine", and ciders, count as alcohol?
decision: Wines by grape or region (chardonnay, merlot, pinot noir, chianti, sangria, port, cava) count; plain "cider" does not (in US recipes it means apple juice), but hard, dry and alcoholic cider, scrumpy and perry do
rationale: Recipes often name the wine itself ("1 cup chardonnay"). Plain cider is unfermented apple juice in the US, where most of these recipes come from; dry cider is the alcoholic UK drink. Port Salut (cheese) is excepted.

question: Does the project ever serve meat from household pets?
decision: No: recipes with dog, cat or guinea pig meat are removed, and the safety filter rejects them for every user
rationale: A choice of the project owner on moral grounds. No such recipe is in the current data; the rule keeps future sources and AI-written recipes out too. Hot dogs, corn dogs, catfish and yukgaejang (a beef soup) are excepted.

question: Are recipes made for pets kept?
decision: No: recipes whose name says they are for animals (dog biscuits, food for dogs, cat treats) are removed
rationale: They are not meals for people, and their ingredients (raw liver, plain meat) would distort the nutrition and cuisine data. Bird-seed breads and trail mixes made for people are kept. Joke names for people food are kept: a recipe with chocolate or alcohol (poisonous to dogs and cats) or with "human" in its name, for example "Dog Food" (a chocolate cereal snack) and "Human Cat Food" (a tuna spread). Refined after checking all 15 Food.com matches by hand (Claude (AI), 2026-10-04).
